items.title: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX
items.summary:
The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at issue clearly authorizes them.

The plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th…
items.t: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

items.title: Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche , a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

Although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services , on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring new significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “ particularly serious crime[s] .”

Tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

Byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

Amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum…
items.t: Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards

items.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
items.summary:
DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy

Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th, energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution, which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment, and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants.

The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. items.title: Trying To Move Thanksgiving Has Not Gone Well, Historically Speaking
items.summary:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day! 

Thanksgiving’s date is set by federal law as the fourth Thursday in November — but that law exists only because a president once tried to move the holiday himself. In 1939, at the urging of retailers who wanted a longer Christmas shopping season, he proclaimed Thanksgiving a week early. States revolted, the calendar descended into chaos, and the rescheduled holiday picked up what mocking nickname? 

Hint: The president was Franklin D. Roosevelt, who did it three years running. The country split — nearly half the states kept the traditional date, and a few observed both — until Congress ended the mess by fixing Thanksgiving in law, choosing the fourth Thursday over the last. 

See the answer on the next page. 

The post Trying To Move Thanksgiving Has Not Gone Well, Historically Speaking appeared first on Above the Law .

items.title: 3 More Questions For A Patent Litigator Turned Legal Recruiter (Part II)
items.summary:
(Image via Getty) 

Last time, I presented Part 1 of my written interview with a former patent litigator turned legal recruiter, Khurram Naik. That column presented his answer to the first of my three questions and focused on the lessons shared by his podcast guests that have relevance to his lateral candidates. What follows are Khurram’s answers to my remaining two questions. As usual, I have added some brief commentary to his answers below, but have otherwise presented his answers as he provided them.

Gaston Kroub: What’s the role of a legal podcast like yours? 

Khurram Naik: Legal media focus on outcomes, like what a court decided in a particular matter. But there’s little insight into the process that led to those outcomes. Lawyers make concerted decisions over a period of time and develop the judgement to direct those outcomes. That’s what the podcast uncovers. 

There is the problem of the vanilla middle. So many interviews with lawyers have rehearsed answers to softball questions. What I’ve found much more interesting are the bookends to the vanilla middle: 1) what are the real challenges and setbacks exceptional lawyers face, and 2) what are the smart calls they’ve made. 

The first inquiry humanizes skilled lawyers so we can actually learn from them. The second inquiry sidesteps the “I’m humbled to announce, it was a team effort, etc.” reaction to discussing successes so we can actually learn what someone did that was skillful. 

Take Rohit Nath ’s interview. As we explored how he was early to the AI copyright disputes, he shared that he had read the Supreme…

Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. items.title: 5 Habits That Keep Great Legal Rainmakers On Top Of Their Game
items.summary:
I’ve been watching tennis for more than 45 years, from Jimmy Connors to Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal, and I still find myself watching Carlos Alcaraz and wondering how he got to a ball I was sure was past him. Then he’ll hit a drop shot from the baseline so soft it barely gets over the net, and I’ll wonder how he even thought to try it. I’ll leave the greatest-of-all-time debate to somebody else, but this guy still shows me things I don’t remember seeing anyone else do. 

There’s no arguing with his natural talent, but what fascinates me is what it takes to get to that level and keep finding ways to get better when everyone else is trying to catch you. I see a version of that in the lawyers I work with. After helping hundreds of attorneys build their books of business, I can tell you that the ones who stay at the top don’t all have the same personality. Some would happily work a room of 200 people, while others would rather spend an hour with one person they genuinely want to know. What they do have in common are five habits that keep working long after their first big year. 

1. Make Business Development A Non-negotiable 

Most lawyers I know say business development is important, but would you know it from looking at their calendars? If the call to a referral partner is the first thing you bump when a client matter heats up, and you never reschedule it, you’ve already decided where business development ranks. The best rainmakers take their commitments to future clients as seriously as they take the work they’re doing for current ones. An urgent matter may force you to…
items.t: 5 Habits That Keep Great Legal Rainmakers On Top Of Their Game

items.title: Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case
items.summary:
With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order , which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

The skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

Lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who said that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

The challengers countered that the question presented is not…

items.title: The People Who Got You Home For Thanksgiving
items.summary:
One Christmas in Chicago, when I was 10 or 11, I got a toolbox. A set of wooden levers held each tool in place. I could turn one, lift out a saw, and get to work, assuming my parents had meant to give a 10-year-old a saw. I chose to assume they had. I just needed something to cut.

The lumberyard a few blocks from our house seemed like the place to start. I walked over with my toolbox and some change and asked the manager if I could buy a few scraps. He asked to see my tools. Now, if you’ve ever given a kid a toolbox, you know the next best present is a chance to open it and show you what’s inside.

That man filled a paper bag with pieces of wood and threw in screws and nails. When I asked what I owed him, he told me to take it. You’d think I could tell you what I built with all that wood. I can’t. But more than 40 years later, I can still see those little levers, and I remember the man who took the time to watch me turn them.

Thanksgiving brings people like him to mind. After nearly 30 years as a lawyer, I could fill a legal pad with the names of people who gave me something I needed at just the right moment. Some would have to think for a minute to remember what they did. That strikes me as a good reason to tell them. For most of us, the list starts pretty close to home.

The last deposition before dinner 

Consider what it takes to get a lawyer home for Thanksgiving. You have a deposition on Wednesday morning. You tell your family you’ll be on the road by lunch, using the same math that lets you tell a judge, “I have just a few more questions.” This time you make it.…
items.t: The People Who Got You Home For Thanksgiving

items.title: ‘The Best Justice System In The World’ Has A Jury Problem
items.summary:
Courtroom dramas give us a reassuring picture of justice: a case goes to trial, a jury hears the evidence, and the right verdict arrives before the credits roll. Real life is considerably less tidy. In The Best Justice System in the World , Suja A. Thomas , a law professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, uses humor to examine how government and corporations can deprive ordinary people of their right to a jury trial. The film is meant to make viewers laugh, then think deeply about what happens when the joke is on someone facing the justice system.

Plea deals can pressure people to give up a jury trial, even when they may be innocent. In civil cases, summary judgment and arbitration can keep discrimination and harassment claims from reaching a jury, too. The film follows people caught in those systems and asks what happens when decisions with life-changing consequences are left to prosecutors, judges, or private arbitrators. Juries remain a familiar fixture on TV. In real life, they can be more of a special guest.

For Thomas, this is personal. The discrimination she and her family experienced helped inspire her to become a lawyer. She later grew concerned that jury trials were becoming increasingly rare. In her director’s statement, she calls juries “a last line of defense” against improper prosecution. That sounds less like legal theory than a warning. The film’s bluntest assessment is even shorter: “We’re f****d.”

Thomas spent decades as a lawyer and law professor trying to draw attention to these issues through articles, books, op-eds, and public…
items.t: ‘The Best Justice System In The World’ Has A Jury Problem

items.title: How LexisNexis Protégé Helps Attorneys Meet Emerging AI Standards
items.summary:
Courts and lawmakers are setting clearer expectations for attorneys’ use of AI. New York’s October 26, 2026, guidance, The Risks of Using Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Court Papers , specifically names LexisNexis® as an authoritative source attorneys can use to independently verify AI-generated citations and quotations. The guidance reinforces attorney accountability under existing duties, without generally requiring special disclosure of AI use under its statewide approach.

California’s SB 574 , signed September 30, 2026, and effective January 1, 2027, adds statutory requirements addressing verification, professional responsibility, confidentiality, and disclosure. Further state action appears likely, although approaches will vary: Pennsylvania’s court advisory committee has published a proposed AI notice and compliance certification for public comment, while New York’s pending S9794 and A9097 would impose additional certification or disclosure obligations. These proposals are not current requirements, but they show that expectations continue to develop.

Across these developments, the expectations can be organized into four practical categories: verify authorities; retain professional responsibility and judgment; protect sensitive information; and document or disclose AI use as applicable. Lexis+® with Protégé™ brings together verification capabilities, attorney-directed skills and drafting tools, and security safeguards that help attorneys address these expectations in their everyday work. items.title: Supreme Court Tries To Skirt State Disclosure Laws Using Your Aunt’s Facebook Privacy Notice
items.summary:
You know that post that your aunt puts up every couple of years about how you need to write “I give notice to Facebook it is strictly forbidden to copy my photos per UCC 1-308, 1-103, and the Rome Statute” or some other vaguely legal wording? It’s gibberish , but it refuses to go away because there’s a healthy mix of genuinely gullible people who like to think it makes sense.

It turns out, the Supreme Court has those people too. And they write email signatures.

According to a new report from Fix the Court , titled “ Broken Records ,” some Supreme Court employees, mostly public information staff and chambers staff, have tacked this language onto their emails since at least the spring of 2022:

“This record, and all records created in response to it, are records of the Supreme Court of the United States, and are not ‘agency records’ under 5 U.S.C. § 552 or similar state statutes. No such records may be disclosed without the prior written approval of the Marshal of the Supreme Court of the United States”

The Supreme Court isn’t an “agency” under federal FOIA, and the Court asserts that its records sit in its “ exclusive legal custody and control .” That’s supposed to keep Court records under wraps. Unless, say, a justice wants to lock in an aggressive draft opinion before his colleagues water it down… hypothetically! 

But the inclusion of “or similar state statutes” and “all records created in response to it,” drifts into sovereign citizen territory of vapid bullshittery. When the Supreme Court corresponds with a state employee and that employee responds, it would and…
items.t: Supreme Court Tries To Skirt State Disclosure Laws Using Your Aunt’s Facebook Privacy Notice

items.title: Biglaw Partner Trades Billable Hours For Alaska’s Attorney General Role
items.summary:
On Monday, Alaska Governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins announced that Jim Torgerson, a partner in Stoel Rives’s Anchorage office, will be the state’s next attorney general. Torgerson isn’t just any partner. The Portland-based Am Law 200 firm named him firm-wide managing partner in January 2016. That made him the first Alaska-based managing partner of an Am Law 200 firm, and he ran the firm until he went back to full-time litigation in Anchorage in 2020. The transition team’s press release says he is “the only Alaska resident to have led a national law firm.” That’s impressive, and it also tells you how many national firms have bothered to plant a flag in Anchorage.

The rest of the résumé is what you’d want from a state’s top lawyer. He has more than four decades of trial experience. He was chief of both the civil and criminal divisions at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Alaska, and he has prosecuted cases for both the state and federal governments. In private practice he has represented Alaska Native corporations, energy and natural resources companies, and individual Alaskans. He also spent the summers of 1980 to 1982 as a temporary Alaska Fish and Wildlife officer in Sitka. Sitka is Kreiss-Tomkins’s hometown, though the 37-year-old governor-elect wouldn’t be born for several more years.

items.title: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism
items.summary:
American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of New England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us .”

At best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the New England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Plan, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment , the juvenile death penalty (until 2005 ), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law. 

A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services , in which the justices will review one of the Trump…
items.t: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

items.title: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?
items.summary:
When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom , Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook , which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

The contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.…
items.t: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

items.title: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?
items.summary:
Last term in Little v. Hecox , which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”

On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

Joseph Lochner : Lochner v. New York 

Let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, New York. He sought employment in the bakery…
items.t: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

items.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
items.summary:
Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next

For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017.

The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel.

Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond

items.title: Is Trump Ever To Blame? Should You Trust Him Or Our Enemies?
items.summary:
(Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images) 

The FAA imposed an aviation ground stop across the entire country a couple of weeks ago, leaving tens of thousands of travelers stranded.

Naturally, the president, as all good leaders do, accepted responsibility.

Ha! Just kidding.

President Donald Trump’s precise words were, “I don’t accept any responsibility.”

What a guy! 

Many of us remember when the country was assigning responsibility for a shortage of COVID tests on the day Trump declared the coronavirus outbreak to be a national emergency. In the words of our noble leader: “I don’t take responsibility at all.”

Of course not.

This got me to thinking: Is Trump consistent about this?

Happily, John Dickerson recently provided the answer, giving examples of the many times Trump has declined responsibility for anything that went wrong in America. Dickerson’s list includes:

In February 2017, after Navy SEAL Ryan Owens died in the first raid (in Yemen) of Trump’s presidency. Trump pointed to the generals who had brought him the plan: “And they lost Ryan.” 

Yes, they did, sir! Responsibility lies with the generals, not the commander-in-chief!

In January 2019, having told Democratic leaders he would “take the mantle” for a government shutdown, Trump paraphrased Harry Truman once the shutdown dragged on: “The buck stops with everybody.” 

On April 27, 2020, when asked whether he bore any responsibility for a spike in poison-hotline calls after he mused about injecting disinfectant: “No, I don’t.” 

And in Spring 2025, when the economy shrank in the first quarter of Trump’s…
items.t: Is Trump Ever To Blame? Should You Trust Him Or Our Enemies?

items.title: The GC’s Superpower Is Changing Altitude
items.summary:
A dashboard says customer commitments are being reviewed on time. An employee keeps a private spreadsheet because the approved system cannot handle a recurring exception.

Both can be true in the same hypothetical company.

The dashboard captures completion. The spreadsheet captures the work required to make completion possible. A GC looking at only one of them has a partial account of the process.

That is why the most useful part of the Shibuya Crossing metaphor is the ability to move between viewpoints. The person above the crossing can see routes. The person walking through it knows which route is blocked, which sign is confusing, and where someone needs more time.

For a general counsel, changing altitude means connecting those forms of knowledge.

At the matter level, you need the particular promise, technical fact, and consequence. At the workflow level, you can examine repeated handoffs and workarounds. At the enterprise level, you can ask which incentives, authorities, and assumptions are producing the pattern.

Each level should inform the others. An executive interpretation that cannot survive contact with an actual matter needs revision.

Research on organizational networks offers a useful connection. In “Structural Holes and Good Ideas,” Ronald Burt examines the value of bridging separated groups. That research supports interest in access to different perspectives. It does not establish that a GC’s title automatically supplies such access.

I would treat the enterprise perspective as something a legal leader must keep earning.

Start by asking a colleague to…
items.t: The GC’s Superpower Is Changing Altitude

items.title: Orrick Matches Cravath On Raises And Bonuses, Translated From Orrick-Speak
items.summary:
Orrick has made its compensation move, and it’s unsurprisingly a full market match, following the standard Cravath finally set last week . That means the $235,000-to-$455,000 salary scale Milbank introduced back in June, plus Cravath’s year-end bonuses, plus Cravath’s newly beefed-up special bonuses.

At least, that’s what it says once you translate it. Orrick doesn’t do class years, so instead of the same chart everyone else uses, they have titles like Associate, Managing Associate, and Senior Associate, each with their own levels. It makes the org chart look a bit more like a Dungeons & Dragons character sheet, but we can basically translate “Level 2 Managing Associate” as a fifth-year.

The memo, from the firm’s talent leadership, opens the way these always open:

Thank you for all your hard work and your commitment to our standards of excellence. It is contributing to an incredibly successful year — in terms of our market impact, client relationships and opportunities to collaborate across our firm.

“Opportunities to collaborate across our firm” is a such a pleasant phrasing for getting staffed on a deal at 11 p.m.

Special bonuses run from $11,000 to $40,000, an exact match for Cravath’s specials , which came in over Milbank’s summer specials of $6,000 to $25,000. Merit bonuses run from $20,000 up to the familiar $115,000. Max it out and the most senior associates take home $155,000 in bonuses, same as at Cravath. Counsel get the top $40,000 special and the $115,000 merit bonus too.

Orrick’s come with this:

Special bonuses will be paid December 31, 2026, to all who…
items.t: Orrick Matches Cravath On Raises And Bonuses, Translated From Orrick-Speak

items.title: The Trump DOJ Pushed Out Its Best Lawyers, Now They Want Jobs Investigating It
items.summary:
For nearly two years, the Trump Justice Department has handled its career lawyers like a disposable resource: fire the ones who worked on the wrong cases, drive out the rest, and backfill with true believers who answer the “forward this to a friend” email. Now a lot of those lawyers are sending their résumés somewhere new… the committee that’s about to investigate the Justice Department.

According to MS NOW, roughly 500 people have applied for investigative and oversight jobs on the House Judiciary Committee, which Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) is set to chair when Democrats take control of the House in January. Per two people familiar with the applications, many of the people hoping to help Raskin probe the Trump DOJ are current or former employees of that same department.

Welp, that tracks.

The DOJ has shed 21 percent of its attorneys , more than 2,600 lawyers, and plenty of them didn’t leave voluntarily. The department fired the prosecutors who worked for Jack Smith, and then went after the ones who enforced federal abortion clinic protections . When it noticed nobody was left to do the work, it dropped the requirement that prosecutors have any legal experience at all , offered $25,000 signing bonuses , and watched its once-prestigious Honors Program struggle to find takers .

A spokesperson for House Judiciary Democrats told MS NOW it’s not a huge surprise that DOJ alums and staff are lining up, and was pretty direct about why:

“The Trump Administration has gutted the federal workforce and driven tens of thousands of highly-experienced nonpartisan civil servants out of…
items.t: The Trump DOJ Pushed Out Its Best Lawyers, Now They Want Jobs Investigating It

items.title: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff. 

***

On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller , in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”

According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

The Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used.…
items.t: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

items.title: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law
items.summary:
In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”

Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.
items.t: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

items.title: The Supreme Court and profanity
items.summary:
Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “ Filthy Words ” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

The station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.” 

Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who…
items.t: The Supreme Court and profanity

items.title: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape
items.summary:
Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said.

In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape

items.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?

After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’

The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter.

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity.
